table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Psychologische Hochschule Berlin (No.

Participants were recruited as part of the "Berlin Study of the AMPD" (for more information, see https://osf.io/bhq94) and a collaborative project investigating the relationship between personality pathology and attachment among psychiatric patients.
table.formatted: Participants were recruited as part of the "Berlin Study of the AMPD" (for more information, see <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/bhq94">https://osf.io/bhq94</ref>) and a collaborative project investigating the relationship between personality pathology and attachment among psychiatric patients.

table.text: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
In the cognitive empathy condition, participants were presented with four emotion adjectives per picture and asked to select the correct answer ("What emotion is this person feeling?").
The MVT consists of 144 trials, in which participants are shown three black-and-white pictures, only one of which depicts a face.
Participants are asked to identify the picture showing a face by clicking on the eyes rather than simply selecting the correct picture.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To evaluate the robustness and interpretability of the main findings, we conducted several supplementary and sensitivity analyses. First, we quantified missing data by estimating the fraction of missing information and approximate effective sample sizes at the model and parameter level. Second, we conducted post hoc power analyses for global model fit and focal parameter estimates. Third, we examined possible violations of key model assumptions, including nonnormality, nonlinearity, and multicollinearity. Fourth, we repeated the main latentmodel analyses using manifest scores with observed cases only to assess the robustness of the findings across modeling approaches. Fifth, we examined sensitivity to parcel composition (systematic alternatives and 500 random allocations) and to the additional residual covariances by omitting them. Finally, we adjusted the central associations for symptom severity by including depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and somatization (PHQ-15) scores as simultaneous manifest covariates.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "To evaluate the robustness and interpretability of the main findings, we conducted several supplementary and sensitivity analyses. First, we quantified missing data by estimating the fraction of missing information and approximate effective sample sizes at the model and parameter level. Second, we conducted post hoc power analyses for global model fit and focal parameter estimates. Third, we examined possible violations of key model assumptions, including nonnormality, nonlinearity, and multicollinearity. Fourth, we repeated the main latentmodel analyses using manifest scores with observed cases only to assess the robustness of the findings across modeling approaches. Fifth, we examined sensitivity to parcel composition (systematic alternatives and 500 random allocations) and to the additional residual covariances by omitting them. Finally, we adjusted the central associations for symptom severity by including depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and somatization (PHQ-15) scores as simultaneous manifest covariates."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .077", Sentence = "Sensitivity analyses excluding the additional residual covariances yielded largely unchanged substantive conclusions, although model fit deteriorated; in Model 6, the association between the specific narcissistic PD factor and crystallized intelligence increased from r = .24 (p = .077) to r = .38 (p = ."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 842 columns across 10 data files.
#### Issues Identified

98 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 9 spreadsheet files in the repository; 5 have at least one formatting issue.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were recruited as part of the "Berlin Study of the AMPD" (for more information, see https://osf.io/bhq94) and a collaborative project investigating the relationship between personality pathology and attachment among psychiatric patients.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
In the cognitive empathy condition, participants were presented with four emotion adjectives per picture and asked to select the correct answer ("What emotion is this person feeling?").
The MVT consists of 144 trials, in which participants are shown three black-and-white pictures, only one of which depicts a face.
Participants are asked to identify the picture showing a face by clicking on the eyes rather than simply selecting the correct picture.

text.text: Personality disorders (PDs) are commonly associated with impairments in social cognition, particularly emotion recognition.

However, evidence also suggests deficits in more basic cognitive functions, including face processing (e.g., detection of non-emotional facial features) and indicators of general intelligence (e.g., crystallized intelligence).

We addressed two exploratory research questions: first, how emotion recognition, face processing, and crystallized intelligence relate to personality pathology across categorical and dimensional PD models, and second, whether these associations primarily reflect general or specific personality pathology.
We further hypothesized that the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition would be attenuated when controlling for face processing or crystallized intelligence.
In a clinical sample (n = 219), cognitive abilities were assessed using performancebased measures, and personality pathology was assessed using interviews and self-reports.
Structural equation modeling, including correlated factor and bifactor-(S-1) models, was applied to separate general from specific personality pathology variance.
General personality pathology showed strong negative associations with emotion recognition and small-to-moderate negative associations with face processing and crystallized intelligence.
Associations with specific personality pathology were substantially attenuated when controlling for general personality pathology.
The link between personality functioning and emotion recognition was only minimally accounted for by face processing or crystallized intelligence.

These findings suggest that cognitive deficits in PD may primarily reflect severity rather than disorder-specific variance, while the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition appears not to be reducible to face processing or crystallized intelligence.
Our study suggests that dimensional models provide a more nuanced framework for understanding cognitive impairment in personality pathology.
Mental disorders are often associated with impairments in cognitive functioning (Abramovitch et al., 2021; Cotter et al., 2018; Millan et al., 2012; Ringwald et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Mental disorders are often associated with impairments in cognitive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abramovitch et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cotter et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Millan et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ringwald et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Personality disorders (PDs) are typically linked to social cognitive dysfunction (Herpertz & Bertsch, 2014), with emotion recognition being one of the most studied domains (Marsden et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2014; Salgado et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Personality disorders (PDs) are typically linked to social cognitive dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Herpertz & Bertsch, 2014)</ref>, with emotion recognition being one of the most studied domains <ref type="bibr">(Marsden et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mitchell et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Salgado et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond emotion recognition, accumulating evidence also points to impairments in broader cognitive domains in PD, including attention, memory, executive functions, face perception, and general intelligence (D'Iorio et al., 2024; Mewton et al., 2025; Sedgwick et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Beyond emotion recognition, accumulating evidence also points to impairments in broader cognitive domains in PD, including attention, memory, executive functions, face perception, and general intelligence <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(D'Iorio et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mewton et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sedgwick et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we focused on two broader cognitive abilities that may help clarify whether deficits in emotion recognition reflect a specifically social-cognitive impairment or broader cognitive dysfunction in PD: indicators of face processing and general intelligence.

As most research on cognitive functioning in PD has focused on single specific PDs (e.g., borderline PD), we adopted a broader perspective by examining both the categorical PD model and the alternative model for PDs (AMPD) in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders -5th Edition (DSM-5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

Current conceptualizations of personality pathology distinguish between general personality pathology, reflecting overall severity of impairment, and specific personality pathology, reflecting stylistic manifestations.
In the AMPD, PDs are defined by impairments in personality functioning (Criterion A) and pathological personality traits (Criterion B).

Personality functioning captures general personality pathology and is operationalized in the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS; Bender et al., 2011), including four domains (identity, selfdirection, empathy, intimacy) that can be further differentiated into twelve subdomains.
text.formatted: Personality functioning captures general personality pathology and is operationalized in the Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bender et al., 2011)</ref>, including four domains (identity, selfdirection, empathy, intimacy) that can be further differentiated into twelve subdomains.

text.text: The AMPD pathological personality trait model (Krueger et al., 2012) represents specific person-ality pathology and comprises 25 trait facets that can be aggregated into five broad trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism).
text.formatted: The AMPD pathological personality trait model <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krueger et al., 2012)</ref> represents specific person-ality pathology and comprises 25 trait facets that can be aggregated into five broad trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism).

text.text: The traditional PD classification in DSM-5 Section II distinguishes between ten specific PDs (antisocial, avoidant, borderline, dependent, histrionic, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive, paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal).
text.formatted: The traditional PD classification in DSM-5 Section II distinguishes between ten specific PDs <ref type="bibr">(antisocial, avoidant, borderline, dependent, histrionic, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive, paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal)</ref>.

text.text: Although this categorical model does not explicitly differentiate between general severity and stylistic trait configurations, the diagnoses reflect specific forms of personality pathology.
Face perception involves extracting different types of information from faces, including identity, facial features, and emotional expression (Haxby et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Face perception involves extracting different types of information from faces, including identity, facial features, and emotional expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Haxby et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we distinguish emotion recognition from face processing in a narrower sense: Whereas emotion recognition may involve facial, contextual, and inferential cues, face processing refers to the perceptual detection of facial features independent of emotional expression.

While emotion recognition has been extensively studied across various mental disorders (Kret & Ploeger, 2015), face processing has been studied less broadly but in greater depth for specific conditions, including autism (Griffin et al., 2021) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (Mewton et al., 2025).
text.formatted: While emotion recognition has been extensively studied across various mental disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kret & Ploeger, 2015)</ref>, face processing has been studied less broadly but in greater depth for specific conditions, including autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Griffin et al., 2021)</ref> and schizophrenia spectrum disorders <ref type="bibr">(Mewton et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Schizotypal PD has been associated with impairments in both emotion recognition and face processing (Mewton et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Schizotypal PD has been associated with impairments in both emotion recognition and face processing <ref type="bibr">(Mewton et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite isolated findings, research on face processing across PDs remains scarce, and direct comparisons with emotion recognition are largely absent.
Intelligence encompasses a range of cognitive abilities that can be captured by a general dimension (Spearman, 1904).
text.formatted: Intelligence encompasses a range of cognitive abilities that can be captured by a general dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Spearman, 1904)</ref>.

text.text: It is traditionally differentiated into fluid intelligence, indicating the capacity to learn and adapt to novel situations, and crystallized intelligence, reflecting accumulated knowledge and skills (Cattell, 1963).
text.formatted: It is traditionally differentiated into fluid intelligence, indicating the capacity to learn and adapt to novel situations, and crystallized intelligence, reflecting accumulated knowledge and skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cattell, 1963)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence on associations between intelligence and PDs remains limited.

Population-based and cohort studies found that lower general intelligence is associated with higher PD prevalence (Weiser et al., 2004) and higher risk for hospitalization in individuals with PD (Gale et al., 2010; Moran et al., 2009; Urfer-Parnas et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Population-based and cohort studies found that lower general intelligence is associated with higher PD prevalence <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Weiser et al., 2004)</ref> and higher risk for hospitalization in individuals with PD <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gale et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Moran et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Urfer-Parnas et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Research on antisocial PD has been more extensive, with meta-analyses reporting small but significant negative associations with general intelligence (Sánchez de Ribera et al., 2019; Sedgwick et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Research on antisocial PD has been more extensive, with meta-analyses reporting small but significant negative associations with general intelligence <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Sánchez de Ribera et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sedgwick et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Two studies in non-clinical samples examined associations between fluid intelligence and PDs, finding negative associations with antisocial, borderline, schizoid, and schizotypal PD (Hengartner et al., 2014; Unsworth et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Two studies in non-clinical samples examined associations between fluid intelligence and PDs, finding negative associations with antisocial, borderline, schizoid, and schizotypal PD <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hengartner et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Unsworth et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Studies in clinical samples are scarce.
To date, there is no evidence on the role of crystallized intelligence in personality pathology, nor on how intelligence more broadly relates to dimensional models of PD.

Taken together, evidence for impaired emotion recognition in personality pathology is relatively well established, whereas studies on face processing and crystallized intelligence in PD remain scarce.

An open question is whether associations between personality pathology and emotion recognition reflect a specific social-cognitive impairment or can be partly explained by more basic cognitive abilities, as suggested by findings that emotion recognition deficits associated with psychopathy may be accounted for by general mental ability (Olderbak et al., 2018).
text.formatted: An open question is whether associations between personality pathology and emotion recognition reflect a specific social-cognitive impairment or can be partly explained by more basic cognitive abilities, as suggested by findings that emotion recognition deficits associated with psychopathy may be accounted for by general mental ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Olderbak et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, because most previous studies have relied on categorical PD models, the extent to which cognitive impairment is primarily linked to specific PDs or to general severity emphasized in dimensional PD models has yet to be clarified.

We recently used the Multifaceted Empathy Test (MET; Foell et al., 2018) to examine impairments in cognitive and emotional empathy as markers of general versus specific personality pathology (Ohse et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We recently used the Multifaceted Empathy Test (MET; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Foell et al., 2018)</ref> to examine impairments in cognitive and emotional empathy as markers of general versus specific personality pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ohse et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A central finding was that general personality pathology was strongly associated with poorer performance in the cognitive empathy condition of the MET, which assesses the recognition of others' emotions in situational contexts.

In the present study, we extended these analyses by including additional cognitive abilities: face processing and crystallized intelligence, assessed with the Mooney-Verhallen-Test (MVT; Verhallen & Mollon, 2016) and the Berlin Test of Fluid and Crystallized Intelligence (BEFKI; Schipolowski et al., 2013a), respectively.
text.formatted: In the present study, we extended these analyses by including additional cognitive abilities: face processing and crystallized intelligence, assessed with the Mooney-Verhallen-Test (MVT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Verhallen & Mollon, 2016)</ref> and the Berlin Test of Fluid and Crystallized Intelligence (BEFKI; <ref type="bibr">Schipolowski et al., 2013a)</ref>, respectively.

text.text: We addressed two exploratory research questions.
First, we examined how emotion recognition, face processing, and crystallized intelligence are associated with personality pathology across categorical and dimensional PD models.
Second, we tested whether these associations primarily reflect general or specific personality pathology.
Given the limited prior evidence, we did not formulate specific hypotheses for these two research questions.

In addition, drawing on the hierarchical structure of face processing (Haxby et al., 2000) and evidence that emotion recognition deficits may reflect general mental ability (Olderbak et al., 2018), we hypothesized that the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition would be attenuated when controlling for face processing and/or crystallized intelligence.
text.formatted: In addition, drawing on the hierarchical structure of face processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Haxby et al., 2000)</ref> and evidence that emotion recognition deficits may reflect general mental ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Olderbak et al., 2018)</ref>, we hypothesized that the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition would be attenuated when controlling for face processing and/or crystallized intelligence.

text.text: >Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Participants were recruited as part of the "Berlin Study of the AMPD" (for more information, see https://osf.io/bhq94) and a collaborative project investigating the relationship between personality pathology and attachment among psychiatric patients.
text.formatted: Participants were recruited as part of the "Berlin Study of the AMPD" (for more information, see <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/bhq94">https://osf.io/bhq94</ref>) and a collaborative project investigating the relationship between personality pathology and attachment among psychiatric patients.

text.text: For the present analyses, only participants who completed the MVT (n = 199), BEFKI (n = 213), or MET (n = 119) were included (total n = 219).

Data were collected between May 2020 and June 2022 in psychotherapy outpatient departments (52.1%), psychiatric inpatient departments (46.1%), through participant referral (1.4%), and via social media (0.5%).

Inclusion criteria were: (a Interview for the AMPD -Module I (SCID-5-AMPD-I; Bender et al., 2018) and completed by 109 participants (49.8%), 44.0% met the empirically derived diagnostic threshold for moderate impairment in personality functioning (Buer Christensen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Inclusion <ref type="formula">criteria were: (a</ref> Interview for the AMPD -Module I (SCID-5-AMPD-I; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bender et al., 2018)</ref> and completed by 109 participants (49.8%), 44.0% met the empirically derived diagnostic threshold for moderate impairment in personality functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Buer Christensen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, 130 participants (59.4%) completed at least one of the two interviews, and among them, 60.0% fulfilled diagnostic criteria for a PD according to either DSM-5 Section II or Criterion A of the AMPD (see Supplementary Table 1).

text.text: According to the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ; Kroenke et al., 2010; Löwe et al., 2002), completed by 215 participants (98.2%), more than half exceeded screening cutoffs for depressive disorders (62.3%), anxiety disorders (57.2%), or somatoform disorders (54.9%).

text.text: All data were collected using the online research platform formr (Arslan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: All data were collected using the online research platform formr <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arslan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The full test battery included additional assessments that were not part of this investigation (for details, see https://osf.io/gzm9d/).
text.formatted: The full test battery included additional assessments that were not part of this investigation (for details, see <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/gzm9d/">https://osf.io/gzm9d/</ref>).

text.text: The tests and self-reports were administered remotely via online links, except for psychiatric inpatients who completed them on-site using a local computer.
Participants received general interview feedback without diagnoses or clinical terminology; attending therapists received written reports upon request.
Financial compensation was provided to participants not recruited from inpatient departments.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Psychologische Hochschule Berlin (No.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
The MET assesses cognitive and emotional empathy using pictures of people in emotionally charged situations (Dziobek et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The MET assesses cognitive and emotional empathy using pictures of people in emotionally charged situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dziobek et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: We used a shortened version (Foell et al., 2018), comprising 40 pictures (20 depicting positive emotions and 20 depicting negative emotions).
text.formatted: We used a shortened version <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Foell et al., 2018)</ref>, comprising 40 pictures (20 depicting positive emotions and 20 depicting negative emotions).

text.text: In the cognitive empathy condition, participants were presented with four emotion adjectives per picture and asked to select the correct answer ("What emotion is this person feeling?").
Correct responses are summed to a total score (range: 0-40).
Although this condition is termed "cognitive empathy" in the MET, we refer to its performance score as "emotion recognition" throughout this study.

More specifically, the score reflects emotion recognition in situational contexts, involving both emotional understanding and broader mental state inference, rather than cognitive empathy in its broader sense.
Emotional empathy scores were not included in the present analyses.
We implemented the MET in formr (for further details, see Ohse et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We implemented the MET in formr (for further details, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Ohse et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The MVT (Verhallen & Mollon, 2016) is a computerized version of the Mooney Face Test (Mooney, 1957), which assesses closure ability with incomplete black-and-white representations of human heads and faces.
text.formatted: The MVT <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Verhallen & Mollon, 2016)</ref> is a computerized version of the Mooney Face Test <ref type="bibr">(Mooney, 1957)</ref>, which assesses closure ability with incomplete black-and-white representations of human heads and faces.

text.text: The MVT consists of 144 trials, in which participants are shown three black-and-white pictures, only one of which depicts a face.
Participants are asked to identify the picture showing a face by clicking on the eyes rather than simply selecting the correct picture.
This innovation reduces the probability of false positives and allows for calculating a score of correctly identified faces (range: 0-144).
Thus, the MVT effectively assesses face processing.
It comprises two parts (A and B), each containing 72 items.
To reduce testing time, we used only part A. The MVT shows excellent parallel-form test and test-retest reliability (Verhallen & Mollon, 2016).
text.formatted: To reduce testing time, we used only part A. The MVT shows excellent parallel-form test and test-retest reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Verhallen & Mollon, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: An internal quality check indicated that a mean reaction time of ≥ 1500 ms per trial was necessary to ensure response validity.
Six of 205 participants fell below this threshold, yielding n = 199.
We implemented the MVT in formr (for implementation instructions, see https://github.com/RobertSchierz/mvt-formr-implementation).
text.formatted: We implemented the MVT in formr (for implementation instructions, see <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/RobertSchierz/mvt-formr-implementation">https://github.com/RobertSchierz/mvt-formr-implementation</ref>).

text.text: The BEFKI (Wilhelm et al., 2014) is a test battery designed to measure various indicators of fluid and crystallized intelligence.
text.formatted: The BEFKI <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Wilhelm et al., 2014)</ref> is a test battery designed to measure various indicators of fluid and crystallized intelligence.

text.text: We administered a short 12-item crystallized intelligence scale derived from this battery for efficient research use (Schipolowski et al., 2013a; Schipolowski et al., 2013b).
text.formatted: We administered a short 12-item crystallized intelligence scale derived from this battery for efficient research use <ref type="bibr">(Schipolowski et al., 2013a;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schipolowski et al., 2013b</ref>).

text.text: Participants answer declarative knowledge questions from the sciences, humanities, and civics.
Each question is presented with four response options, of which one is correct, yielding a sum score ranging from 0 to 12.
We implemented the BEFKI in formr by presenting the 12 items in random order with a 25-second time limit to reduce cheating.
Of the 215 participants who started the test, two were excluded for not completing the test link, yielding n = 213.
Among these, 139 completed all items within the time limit, while 74 missed at least one.
Unanswered items were coded as incorrect.
The SCID-5-AMPD-I (Bender et al., 2018; Hörz-Sagstetter et al., 2025) is a semi-structured interview assessing personality functioning according to Criterion A of the AMPD.
text.formatted: The SCID-5-AMPD-I <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bender et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hörz-Sagstetter et al., 2025)</ref> is a semi-structured interview assessing personality functioning according to Criterion A of the AMPD.

text.text: The twelve LPFS subdomains are rated by trained clinicians on a 5-point scale ranging from 0 (little or no impairment) to 4 (extreme impairment).
These ratings can be aggregated into the four domains (identity, self-direction, empathy, intimacy) and the global level of personality functioning.
The SCID-5-AMPD-I has proven to be reliable and valid (for detailed information on reliability estimates and interviewer training in the present sample, see Ohse et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The SCID-5-AMPD-I has proven to be reliable and valid (for detailed information on reliability estimates and interviewer training in the present sample, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Ohse et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The SCID-5-PD (Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019) is a semi-structured interview designed to diagnose the ten DSM-5 Section II PDs.

For each PD, seven to nine A-criteria are rated on a 3-point scale (0 = criterion not met,1 = criterion subclinically met,2 = criterion met), and a minimum number of criteria must receive a rating of 2 to establish a diagnosis.
Participants meeting ≥ 10 A-criteria across categories without fulfilling any specific PD received the diagnosis "PD not otherwise specified" (Pagan et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Participants meeting ≥ 10 A-criteria across categories without fulfilling any specific PD received the diagnosis "PD not otherwise specified" <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Pagan et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The criteria can be averaged dimensionally (range = 0-2) to yield individual PD scores.
The SCID-5-PD has good interrater reliability for both dimensional and categorical scores (Somma et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The SCID-5-PD has good interrater reliability for both dimensional and categorical scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Somma et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The LPFS -Self Report (LPFS-SR; Morey, 2017; Zimmermann et al., 2020) captures personality functioning with 80 items, rated on a 4-point scale (ranging from totally false, not at all true to very true) and weighted according to the severity of impairment they represent.
text.formatted: The LPFS -Self Report (LPFS-SR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Morey, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Zimmermann et al., 2020</ref>) captures personality functioning with 80 items, rated on a 4-point scale (ranging from totally false, not at all true to very true) and weighted according to the severity of impairment they represent.

text.text: Weighted item scores can be aggregated to yield scores for the four domains and overall level of personality functioning.
Studies have confirmed its reliability (Hopwood et al., 2018), and structural and construct validity (Uliaszek et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Studies have confirmed its reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hopwood et al., 2018)</ref>, and structural and construct validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Uliaszek et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5; Krueger et al., 2012; Zimmermann et al., 2014) is the standard self-report of AMPD pathological personality traits, consisting of 25 trait facets that can be grouped into five domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism).
text.formatted: The Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Krueger et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Zimmermann et al., 2014)</ref> is the standard self-report of AMPD pathological personality traits, consisting of 25 trait facets that can be grouped into five domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism).

text.text: Items are rated on a 4-point scale from 0 (very false) to 3 (very true).
In the present study, the shorter 100-item PID-5-SF (Maples et al., 2015) was used.
text.formatted: In the present study, the shorter 100-item PID-5-SF <ref type="bibr">(Maples et al., 2015)</ref> was used.

text.text: The PID-5 has well-established psychometric properties (Freilich et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The PID-5 has well-established psychometric properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Freilich et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: All analyses were performed using structural equation modeling (SEM) in R (version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025) with the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) and maximum likelihood estimation with scaled test statistic and robust standard errors.
text.formatted: All analyses were performed using structural equation modeling (SEM) in R (version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025) with the lavaan package <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref> and maximum likelihood estimation with scaled test statistic and robust standard errors.

text.text: Because data collection took place across different sites where not all measures were administered, the number of completed assessments varied: MET (n = 119), MVT (n = 199), BEFKI (n = 213), SCID-5-AMPD-I (n = 109), SCID-5-PD (n = 129), LPFS-SR (n = 217), and PID-5-SF (n = 216).
Missing data were handled using full information maximum likelihood to retain the full sample (n = 219).
Model fit was evaluated using the comparative fit index (CFI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR).
Model fit was considered good if CFI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06, and SRMR ≤ .08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999), and acceptable if CFI ≥ .90 and RMSEA ≤ .08 (Brown, 2015).
text.formatted: Model fit was considered good if CFI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06, and SRMR ≤ .08 <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hu & Bentler, 1999)</ref>, and acceptable if CFI ≥ .90 and RMSEA ≤ .08 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Latent variables were estimated with aggregate indicators because constructs were defined at the scale or domain level and item-level SEMs would have required substantially more parameters relative to sample size.
Personality functioning was represented by eight domain scores, comprising the four domains from both the SCID-5-AMPD-I and LPFS-SR.
The five pathological personality trait domains were each defined by their three standard PID-5-SF facet scores.
Item parcels were constructed for the three cognitive measures and the SCID-5-PD.
Cognitive items were allocated sequentially to four 18-item MVT parcels, four 3-item BEFKI parcels, and four 10-item MET parcels (two per valence).
For each DSM-5 Section II PD, criteria with (near-)zero variance were excluded before sequentially allocating retained criteria to two approximately equally sized parcels.
Supplementary Table 2 details the exact item and criterion composition.
text.formatted: Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref> details the exact item and criterion composition.

text.text: In the first step, we estimated confirmatory correlated factor models.
Model 1 included only the three cognitive ability factors to examine their intercorrelations.
Subsequently, we estimated correlated factor models to examine their bivariate associations with personality functioning, pathological personality traits, and DSM-5 PDs (Model 2-4).
Model 2 included a global personality functioning factor (SCID-5-AMPD-I, LPFS-SR).
To account for method effects, indicators from the same instrument were allowed to correlate.
Model 3 entailed the five pathological personality trait domains.

To improve model fit, three residual covariances among indicators within trait domains were freely estimated (anxiousness with separation insecurity; deceitfulness with grandiosity; withdrawal with intimacy avoidance).
Model 4 comprised the DSM-5 PDs.
Because each PD was represented by only two parcels, both loadings on each PD factor were fixed to 1 to ensure local identification.
A correlated factors model including all ten PDs as latent variables did not converge to a proper solution.

All but two PDs (paranoid and schizotypal PD) could be included in the model when allowing the residual variances of the two antisocial PD parcels to correlate with the residual variance of the second narcissistic PD parcel, consistent with conceptual overlap in antagonistic/externalizing personality pathology.

Paranoid PD could additionally be included by z-standardizing all indicators in the model and by specifying the paranoid PD factor using the total paranoid PD score as a single indicator, fixing its residual variance to 1 -r, where r is the reliability estimate (Brown, 2015).
text.formatted: Paranoid PD could additionally be included by z-standardizing all indicators in the model and by specifying the paranoid PD factor using the total paranoid PD score as a single indicator, fixing its residual variance to 1 -r, where r is the reliability estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the interrater reliability estimate of .85 for paranoid PD reported by Lobbestael et al. (2011), the residual variance of the total paranoid PD score was fixed to .15.
text.formatted: Based on the interrater reliability estimate of .85 for paranoid PD reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lobbestael et al. (2011)</ref>, the residual variance of the total paranoid PD score was fixed to .15.

text.text: In the second step, we examined associations between the three cognitive ability factors and personality pathology distinguishing general from specific personality pathology variance using bifactor-(S-1) models (Eid et al., 2017; Heinrich et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the second step, we examined associations between the three cognitive ability factors and personality pathology distinguishing general from specific personality pathology variance using bifactor-(S-1) models <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Eid et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Heinrich et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the correlated factor models, we specified two bifactor-(S-1) models with a general PD (GPD) factor defined by indicators of personality functioning; within-method residual covariances among personality functioning indicators, as in Model 2, were retained.
These models included five specific pathological personality trait domain factors (Model 5) and eight specific PDs (excluding paranoid and schizotypal PD due to convergence problems; Model 6).

To improve fit, residual covariances were added sequentially based on modification indices and conceptual overlap: nine in Model 5 (see Figure 1) and 16 in Model 6 (12 cross-PD, four cross-method; see Figure 2).
text.formatted: To improve fit, residual covariances were added sequentially based on modification indices and conceptual overlap: nine in Model 5 (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>) and 16 in Model 6 (12 cross-PD, four cross-method; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: The residual covariances of Models 5-6 were used to account for local dependencies rather than interpreted substantively (see Supplementary Table 3 for the specific residual covariances and their conceptual rationales).
text.formatted: The residual covariances of Models 5-6 were used to account for local dependencies rather than interpreted substantively (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">3</ref> for the specific residual covariances and their conceptual rationales).

text.text: In both bifactor-(S-1) models, the specific factors were orthogonal to the GPD factor and to each other.
The three cognitive ability factors were estimated separately and allowed to correlate with the GPD factor, the specific factors, and with each other (see Figures 1 2).
text.formatted: The three cognitive ability factors were estimated separately and allowed to correlate with the GPD factor, the specific factors, and with each other (see Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: In the third step, we used two latent partial correlation models to test whether the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition was accounted for by face processing (Model 7) or crystallized intelligence (Model 8).
Again, personality functioning was specified by eight indicators (SCID-5-AMPD-I, LPFS-SR), with correlations allowed between indicators from the same instrument.
In both models, the latent emotion recognition factor (MET) was regressed on the respective secondary cognitive ability factor (MVT or BEFKI).

The personality functioning factor was allowed to correlate with both the secondary factor and the residual of the emotion recognition factor; the latter correlation represents the partial association controlling for the secondary factor (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: The personality functioning factor was allowed to correlate with both the secondary factor and the residual of the emotion recognition factor; the latter correlation represents the partial association controlling for the secondary factor (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: To evaluate the robustness and interpretability of the main findings, we conducted several supplementary and sensitivity analyses.
First, we quantified missing data by estimating the fraction of missing information and approximate effective sample sizes at the model and parameter level.
Second, we conducted post hoc power analyses for global model fit and focal parameter estimates.
Third, we examined possible violations of key model assumptions, including nonnormality, nonlinearity, and multicollinearity.
Fourth, we repeated the main latentmodel analyses using manifest scores with observed cases only to assess the robustness of the findings across modeling approaches.
Fifth, we examined sensitivity to parcel composition (systematic alternatives and 500 random allocations) and to the additional residual covariances by omitting them.
Finally, we adjusted the central associations for symptom severity by including depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and somatization (PHQ-15) scores as simultaneous manifest covariates.

text.text: In Model 1, emotion recognition was highly correlated with crystallized intelligence (r = .51), whereas face processing showed small-to-moderate correlations with both emotion recognition (r = .24) and crystallized intelligence (r = .28).

Across Models 2-4, impaired emotion recognition was significantly associated with most personality pathology domains, most prominently with personality functioning (r = -.54), paranoid PD (r = -.57), dependent PD (r = -.55), and psychoticism (r = -.48).
Most other correlations with trait domains and specific PDs were in the moderate range (r = -.19 to -.43).
Deficits in face processing had significant correlations with personality functioning (r = -.28), schizoid PD (r = -.39), and obsessive-compulsive PD (r = -.33).
In all other cases, correlations between face processing and personality pathology were small to negligible (r = -.17 to .18).
Lower crystallized intelligence was significantly associated with personality functioning (r = -.27), psychoticism (r = -.30), and avoidant PD (r = -.38).
Correlations with remaining trait domains and specific PDs were small to negligible (r = -.20 to .14).
Both bifactor-(S-1) models (Models 5-6) showed acceptable fit (see Table 1).

After controlling for the GPD factor, the specific personality pathology factors (i.e., residual variance independent of GPD) showed no statistically significant associations with emotion recognition or crystallized intelligence.

In contrast, face processing remained significantly associated with the specific (GPD-independent) variance of obsessive-compulsive PD (r = -.29), disinhibition (r = .33), borderline PD (r = .27), histrionic PD (r = .37), and narcissistic PD (r = .35).

text.text: In the present study, we investigated associations between impaired cognitive functioning and general/specific personality pathology, with a particular focus on whether associations between general personality pathology and emotion recognition were accounted for by face processing and/or crystallized intelligence.

Building on our previous study using partly overlapping data (Ohse et al., 2024), we replicated associations between impaired emotion recognition and personality pathology, including strong associations with general personality pathology (r = -.51).
text.formatted: Building on our previous study using partly overlapping data <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ohse et al., 2024)</ref>, we replicated associations between impaired emotion recognition and personality pathology, including strong associations with general personality pathology (r = -.51).

text.text: Despite similar effect sizes to our previous study, associations with specific personality pathology were not statistically significant in the present bifactor models.

Our findings are consistent with meta-analytic evidence documenting emotion recognition deficits in borderline PD (Daros et al., 2013; Mitchell et al., 2014), but suggest that these deficits may not be specific to borderline pathology.
text.formatted: Our findings are consistent with meta-analytic evidence documenting emotion recognition deficits in borderline PD <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Daros et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mitchell et al., 2014)</ref>, but suggest that these deficits may not be specific to borderline pathology.

text.text: In our bifactor models, borderline PD was no longer sig-nificantly associated with emotion recognition after controlling for general personality pathology, indicating that such deficits may reflect general personality pathology rather than a borderline-specific impairment.
Our analyses involving associations of personality pathology with face processing and crystallized intelligence were exploratory.
We found significant small-to-moderate associations between personality functioning/general personality pathology and deficits in both cognitive abilities (r = -.19 to -.28).
These findings are novel.

Nonetheless, they align with the broader literature on cognitive deficits in PD, including meta-analytic evidence linking borderline PD to deficits in memory, attention, inhibition, and executive functioning (D'Iorio et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, they align with the broader literature on cognitive deficits in PD, including meta-analytic evidence linking borderline PD to deficits in memory, attention, inhibition, and executive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(D'Iorio et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our results also indicate that some cognitive deficits may be overlooked when focusing on specific PDs.

In our data, impairments in face processing and crystallized intelligence were primarily associated with general personality pathology, whereas associations with specific PDs were less prominent or no longer evident when general personality pathology was taken into account.

Looking more closely at these specific associations, we found that deficits in face processing were significantly correlated with schizoid and obsessive-compulsive PD, whereas lower crystallized intelligence was significantly correlated with psychoticism and avoidant PD.

However, when controlling for general personality pathology, none of these correlations remained statistically significant, except for the association between face processing and obsessive-compulsive PD.

Previous research examining associations between these cognitive abilities and personality pathology is scarce and has mostly focused on specific PDs, with notable evidence available only for impaired face processing in schizotypal PD (Mewton et al., 2025) and reduced general intelligence in antisocial PD (Sánchez de Ribera et al., 2019; Sedgwick et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Previous research examining associations between these cognitive abilities and personality pathology is scarce and has mostly focused on specific PDs, with notable evidence available only for impaired face processing in schizotypal PD <ref type="bibr">(Mewton et al., 2025)</ref> and reduced general intelligence in antisocial PD <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Sánchez de Ribera et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sedgwick et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We could not corroborate these specific associations.

This may partly reflect that schizotypal PD could not be included in our factor analytic models due to estimation problems and that general intelligence was operationalized using only a single indicator (i.e., crystallized intelligence) rather than a comprehensive measure.
Moreover, our sample included only four individuals who met criteria for antisocial PD and none who met criteria for schizotypal PD.
That said, our primary aim was not to replicate findings on specific PDs, but to examine personality pathology more broadly by including dimensional PD models.

Although further research is needed, our findings suggest that dimensional rather than categorical models of PD provide a more nuanced framework for examining (social) cognitive functioning in personality pathology.
Contrary to our hypothesis, the association between personality functioning and emotion recognition was only slightly attenuated when controlling for face processing or crystallized intelligence.
This contrasts with evidence that emotion recognition deficits associated with psychopathy were fully accounted for by general mental ability (Olderbak et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This contrasts with evidence that emotion recognition deficits associated with psychopathy were fully accounted for by general mental ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Olderbak et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The divergence may reflect conceptual differences between psychopathy and general personality pathology, as well as distinctions between general mental ability and the more specific cognitive domains we assessed.
Moreover, the MET may capture a more contextualized and inferential form of emotion recognition rather than the more narrowly face-focused tasks used by Olderbak et al. (2018).
text.formatted: Moreover, the MET may capture a more contextualized and inferential form of emotion recognition rather than the more narrowly face-focused tasks used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Olderbak et al. (2018)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, our findings suggest that emotion recognition, face processing, and crystallized intelligence relate to personality functioning through partially independent mechanisms.

From a neurobiological perspective, this pattern is consistent with models proposing distributed neural systems underlying different aspects of face and semantic processing (Binder & Desai, 2011; Haxby et al., 2000).
text.formatted: From a neurobiological perspective, this pattern is consistent with models proposing distributed neural systems underlying different aspects of face and semantic processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Binder & Desai, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Haxby et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The relative independence of these domains may therefore reflect differentiated neural systems linking general personality pathology to distinct cognitive functions.
Some limitations should be noted.

First, certain forms of specific personality pathology that have previously been associated with deficits in face processing (e.g., schizotypal PD) and reduced general intelligence (e.g., antisocial PD) were scarcely represented or entirely absent in the current sample.
Second, intelligence was captured only with the verbally weighted BE-FKI crystallized intelligence scale and fluid intelligence was not assessed, limiting conclusions about intelligence more broadly.
Third, incomplete assessments reduced the information available: of 219 participants, 119 completed the MET, 109 the SCID-5-AMPD-I, and 129 the SCID-5-PD.
Full information maximum likelihood used all available data but could not fully compensate for missing information.
MET and interview-based associations require caution, particularly non-significant findings for specific personality pathology.
Reduced effective sample sizes may also have contributed to estimation problems in complex models.
Fourth, the MET assesses contextual emotion recognition involving emotional understanding and mental state inference.

It may capture general social-cognitive difficulties more readily than disorderspecific patterns, potentially contributing to the limited specific associations after accounting for general personality pathology.
These findings therefore do not rule out disorder-specific emotion recognition difficulties.
General personality pathology showed strong associations with impaired emotion recognition and small-to-moderate associations with face processing deficits and lower crystallized intelligence.

Associations between specific personality pathology and cognitive abilities were largely attenuated when controlling for general personality pathology, suggesting that cognitive dysfunction in PD primarily reflects severity of personality pathology.
However, this interpretation remains tentative because methodological constraints may have obscured disor-der-specific associations.

The association between personality functioning and emotion recognition remained strong after controlling for face processing or crystallized intelligence, suggesting it is not reducible to these abilities.
Overall, dimensional PD models may provide a more nuanced framework for understanding cognitive impairment in personality pathology.

Exclusion criteria were: (a) cognitive deficits due to substance use, acute psychosis, intellectual disability, or medication; (b) acute suicidality; and (c) insufficient German language proficiency.
Mean age was 34.9 years (SD = 11.8; range: 19.0-65.8).
Most were female (63.9%).
About one third (29.2%) held a university degree.
Less than half (43.4%) were taking psychotropic drugs.
According to the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 -PDs (SCID-5-PD; Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019), completed by 129 participants (58.9%), 50.4% met criteria for a DSM-5 Section II PD.

Original allocation refers to the parcel composition used in the primary analyses.
The alternating and random allocations displayed in the table varied cognitive items only and retained the original residual-covariance specification.
Alternating allocation distributed items cyclically across parcels while preserving the separation of positive-and negative-valence MET items.
In the mixed-valence MET condition, each of the four MET parcels comprised five positive-and five negative-valence items; all other parcels were unchanged.
Random-allocation results are medians and 2.5th-97.5th percentiles across admissible solutions from 500 allocations and reflect variability across parcel allocations rather than confidence intervals.
Parcel sizes were held constant, and random cognitive allocations preserved the separation of positive-and negative-valence MET items.

Additional analyses reallocating SCID-5-PD criteria omitted PD parcel-to-parcel residual covariances and used the original allocation under the same reduced specification as the reference; PF method covariances were retained.

In Model 6, random PD-only allocations yielded similar associations of GPD with MET, MVT, and BEFKI (median rs = -.511, -.227, and -.238, respectively; corresponding reduced-reference rs = -.521, -.235, and -.233; 479/500 admissible solutions).
